title: Is this split really fifty-fifty?
hook: The same split percentages appear in a thousand users and a million.

knows: arithmetic means, rates and simple plotted values
doesNotKnow: a 50/50 test that ends 50.8/49.2 with millions of users signals a bug, not luck.

misconception: Treating sample ratio mismatch as valid without checking the stated model, denominators or causal assumptions.
objective: a 50/50 test that ends 50.8/49.2 with millions of users signals a bug, not luck.
keyState: Both finite cases completed; their computed summaries retained.

claims.text: A 50/50 test ends with 508,000 and 492,000 users. For expected 500,000 each, what is the Pearson χ² allocation statistic?
claims.source: src/demos/probability/p100-sample-ratio-mismatch/spec.ts; exact finite illustration specified in manager numericCase: Expected counts500/500. Observed508/492 chi-square.256 (not alarming); scaled508000/492000 chi-square256 (alarming). Make denominator visible. Avoid saying any deviation proves bug.

claims.text: The million-user case retains χ²=256; the thousand-user case retains 0.256. Both have the same percentage split, but the larger denominator makes that deviation much more surprising under a 50/50 model.
claims.source: src/demos/probability/p100-sample-ratio-mismatch/spec.ts; exact finite illustration specified in manager numericCase: Expected counts500/500. claims.text: An allocation mismatch is a diagnostic signal, not proof of one particular bug. Check assignment, eligibility and logging before interpreting outcome differences from the affected experiment.
claims.source: src/demos/probability/p100-sample-ratio-mismatch/spec.ts; exact finite illustration specified in manager numericCase: Expected counts500/500. claims.text: Holding the observed split percentages fixed, multiplying total sample size by ten does what to χ²? Observed-minus-expected counts scale tenfold; squared deviations divided by expected counts therefore scale tenfold.
